passage: Snow had stopped the trains in Helsinki, and Alka's plan for a Diwali dinner shrank to the five people who could walk. The electricity flickered once and died. Alka lit the diyas that were meant only as decoration and used them to see. Down the hall, Hrithik knocked with a bag of naan from the last open shop. Two friends from the language class arrived stamping snow off their boots, one carrying a pot of rice, the other a story about a grandmother's festival in Lagos. They ate by candlelight, in a mix of Hindi, English and one shared Finnish greeting. Alka looked at the messy table and realised nobody there shared the same ancestors, but they shared this evening, and for the first time in months the flat felt like home.

qa.q: What had stopped the trains in Helsinki?
qa.a: Snow had stopped the trains in Helsinki.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling at the messy table?
qa.a: Warm and at home, realising that belonging came from shared time, not shared ancestry.

qa.q: What made the evening work despite the storm?
qa.a: Adapting the plan to the five who could walk over and using the diyas for light.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have felt bringing naan through the snow?
qa.a: Glad to contribute and to belong, since Hrithik made the effort to reach the group.

grounding: A young adult far from home builds a chosen circle around a festival meal, showing belonging built through shared time.

passage: On the first Sunday of every month, Tenzin's small Mumbai flat filled with people far from home: Jasleen from Ludhiana, a colleague from Guwahati, two students from Kochi. Each brought something: Jasleen's parathas, Tenzin's momos, a pot of fish curry. Nobody was related, and nobody had to explain a pause before a word in a mother tongue. Jasleen taught a Punjabi phrase for eat more and everyone tried it. Last month, when Tenzin's grandmother was unwell in Gangtok and Tenzin sat silent, Jasleen simply refilled the tea and stayed until midnight. Nothing was said about it. The next month a small brass bell appeared on the shelf, brought by whoever felt like it.

qa.q: How often does the group meet?
qa.a: The group meets on the first Sunday of every month.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling while sitting silent, and how did Jasleen's action help?
qa.a: Worried and alone; Jasleen's staying and refilling the tea eased the loneliness.

qa.q: What makes this circle work?
qa.a: Shared time and small kindnesses, like a potluck and phrases from each language.

qa.q: Why might Jasleen have said nothing about staying until midnight?
qa.a: Because the kindness needed no words; staying was enough to show care.

grounding: A young adult far from home builds a circle of friends around shared meals, languages and kindness.

passage:
"Vaibhav, you're making too many pithas. Who's eating all this?"
"Everyone, Tanuja. I invited the whole floor for Bihu."
"The whole floor? You don't even know the guy in 403."
"I know he's from Kerala and his parents are far too. And the girls in 406 are from Manipur and Rajasthan."
"So it's a Bihu party with no Assamese people except you?"
"Exactly. That's the point." Vaibhav wiped his hands. "Last year I spent Bihu alone watching my mother on video. I cried like a baby."
Tanuja softened. "Okay. What can I do?"
"Make your Maharashtrian thecha. Every Bihu needs something spicy."
At seven, the doorbell kept ringing. The guy from 403 brought banana chips. The girls brought ghevar. Someone played Bihu songs from a phone, and everyone danced badly. Tanuja watched Vaibhav laughing in the middle and thought: he built this.

qa.q: What did the guy from 403 bring?
qa.a: Banana chips.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when he remembered last year's Bihu?
qa.a: He felt lonely and homesick, crying while watching his mother on video.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do that built belonging?
qa.a: He invited neighbours from different places to share his festival and asked each to bring something, turning his homesickness into a shared celebration.

qa.q: How does Tanuja see Vaibhav by the end of the evening?
qa.a: Tanuja sees him with new respect, recognising that he built a community out of strangers.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult far from home who builds a circle through a shared festival meal, showing belonging made by shared time.

passage:
When I first moved to Dublin for my nursing job, two years ago, the loneliness surprised me. I, Vidya, would come home from night shifts, eat curd rice alone and cry on the phone to Amma. By the first Onam, I couldn't bear it.
So I did a slightly mad thing. I put a note in the hospital staff room: "Onam lunch on Sunday. Bring nothing, just come." Nine people came: two Filipino nurses, an Irish porter named Declan, Vishal from pharmacy who was from Pune, a Nigerian doctor and her kids. We ate off banana leaves I'd found in an Asian shop. Declan tried to eat rice with his hand and got it everywhere.
Now we meet every month, rotating homes: Filipino adobo, Nigerian jollof, Vishal's mother's poha recipe. They're not my family. But when I had flu last winter, they took turns bringing soup. That's family enough.

qa.q: How many people came to the first Onam lunch?
qa.a: Nine people came.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel in the first months in Dublin?
qa.a: Vidya felt lonely and homesick, crying on the phone to Amma after night shifts.

qa.q: What step would you suggest to someone else far from home, based on Vidya's story?
qa.a: Invite others to share a festival or meal, even strangers from different places, and keep meeting regularly so the group becomes a real circle.

qa.q: How might Declan experience these monthly meals?
qa.a: Declan probably enjoys them and feels included, even laughing at his messy attempt at eating rice by hand.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult far from home who builds a chosen community through shared meals and kindness.

passage:
Warden's note, Srinivasa Working Professionals' Hostel, Bengaluru.
Yogesh moved in last June from a small town in Maharashtra. For the first two months he kept to his room, ate alone, and I often saw him on the terrace on video calls, looking low. In September he asked if he could use the common kitchen on Sundays. The first week, he made pav bhaji and knocked on doors. Only two came: Amandeep from Ludhiana and a quiet boy from Assam. The next Sunday there were six.
Now Sunday dinner is a fixture. Each week someone cooks food from their home state. Amandeep did makki roti in November. Nobody shares a language fully; they switch between Hindi, English and bad Kannada. When one boy's father was in hospital, the group sat with him through the night. I have started keeping extra vessels in the kitchen for them.

qa.q: What did Yogesh make the first week?
qa.a: Pav bhaji.

qa.q: How did Yogesh seem to feel in his first two months at the hostel?
qa.a: He seemed lonely and low, keeping to his room, eating alone and taking video calls on the terrace.

qa.q: What made Yogesh's Sunday dinners work?
qa.a: He kept inviting people, let everyone cook food from home, and the regular meals grew into real care, like sitting up with a friend whose father was in hospital.

qa.q: How might Amandeep see the Sunday dinners?
qa.a: Amandeep probably feels at home in them, having cooked makki roti and joined from the very first week.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult far from home who builds a circle through shared festival and home food, showing belonging made by shared time.

passage:
14 January
Pongal, a whole ocean away from Madurai, and I almost skipped it. Decided at 6 am, half asleep: no. I'm not eating curd rice alone again.
Texted everyone. Leela brought her rice cooker and her Malayalam playlist. Tomasz from the lab brought poppy-seed cake, "because festivals need cake". Mrs Okafor from downstairs came with jollof rice and stayed three hours. We boiled the pongal till it spilled over, and I made everyone shout "Pongalo pongal!" Tomasz shouted loudest, and wrongest.
Amma called during the washing up and heard the noise. "Who are all these people?" My people, I said. It came out before I could think.
In April Leela wants to do Vishu, and Tomasz is already asking about Easter. I think we have a calendar now.
— Keerthana

qa.q: What did Tomasz bring to the Pongal meal?
qa.a: Tomasz brought poppy-seed cake, because festivals need cake.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel at 6 am before deciding to invite everyone?
qa.a: Keerthana felt lonely and low, half ready to skip the festival rather than eat curd rice alone again.

qa.q: What step turned a lonely festival into a shared one?
qa.a: Keerthana texted everyone early instead of waiting to be invited, which gave friends from different places a reason to bring food and share the day.

qa.q: What is it like for Amma to hear the noise during the call?
qa.a: Amma is surprised by all the voices, and may feel comforted that Keerthana is not alone so far from Madurai.

grounding: Shows a young adult far from home building a circle of friends around a shared festival meal, making belonging out of shared time.
